one_liner: Drinking that a person can't control and keeps up despite harm to health, work, safety, or relationships.
in_simple_words: Alcohol use disorder ranges from mild to severe. It's not about what you drink or whether you drink daily; it's about losing control: drinking more than planned, failing to cut down, craving, needing more, withdrawal, and carrying on despite the damage. It's one of the most common mental health conditions and one of the most hidden. Stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous, so medical advice matters. Treatment works, and millions of people are in recovery.
what_it_can_feel_like: I never drank in the morning, so I told myself I was fine. I just couldn't stop once I started.
The shakes in the morning were the thing I couldn't explain away.
A year sober. I'm not 'cured'. I'm free, one day at a time, with a lot of help.
common_signs: Drinking more, or more often, than intended
Trying to cut down and not managing
Cravings, or needing more to feel the same effect
Shakes, sweats, anxiety, or poor sleep when not drinking
Drinking despite health, money, work, or relationship problems
Hiding drinking or feeling defensive about it

myths_vs_facts.myth: You're only an alcoholic if you drink in the morning or lose your job.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most people with alcohol use disorder are working, parenting, and functioning. 'High-functioning' doesn't mean no harm.
Alcohol changes the brain's reward and stress systems. Treatment, medication, and support beat willpower alone.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Stopping cold turkey is the brave way.
myths_vs_facts.fact: For heavy daily drinkers, sudden stopping can cause seizures and can be fatal. Medically supervised withdrawal is the safe way.

how_common.plain: About 1 in 10 people aged 12 and over in the US had alcohol use disorder in the past year, nearly 29 million people.
how_common.figure: 28.9 million people (10.2%) aged 12+ with past-year alcohol use disorder (NSDUH 2023)

what_helps.plain_summary: Options range from brief advice and self-help for milder problems to specialist treatment for dependence. Talking therapies (CBT, motivational approaches, behavioural couples therapy) help. Three medications, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, reduce cravings or relapse. Medically supervised withdrawal is needed for heavy dependence. Mutual-aid groups like AA and SMART Recovery support long-term recovery, and family programmes like Al-Anon support relatives.
evidence_based_options: Brief interventions and guided self-help for harmful drinking
CBT, motivational enhancement, and behavioural couples therapy
Medications to support abstinence or reduce drinking, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Medically supervised withdrawal, then relapse prevention and mutual-aid groups
self_help_that_supports_care: Tracking drinks honestly for two weeks
Alcohol-free days, then stretches, with support
Telling people you're cutting down so they stop pouring
Meetings, online or local; try several

when_to_reach_out: If you've tried to cut down and can't, drink to cope, or get shaky or anxious when you stop, talk to a doctor or an alcohol helpline. Do not stop suddenly after heavy daily drinking without medical advice. Get emergency help for seizures, confusion, or hallucinations when stopping.
is_not: Drinking above recommended limits is risky but isn't a disorder on its own. Binge drinking at parties, without loss of control the rest of the time, is harmful but different from dependence.
hope_note: People recover from severe alcohol use disorder every day. Recovery communities are full of people who thought they were the exception.

content_notes: No dosing, sourcing, or 'how to use' detail. Harm-reduction pointers only to official organizations.
Crisis strip with substance helplines required.

in_young_people: Teenage drinking is common and most teens don't develop a disorder, but early heavy drinking raises the risk. Family involvement and treating the anxiety or trauma underneath matter most.
across_cultures: Drinking norms vary hugely: alcohol is forbidden in some faiths and central to social life in some cultures. Shame about drinking problems is universal. Culturally specific recovery programmes exist in many communities, including Indigenous-led ones.

sub_sections.title: Alcohol intoxication and withdrawal
sub_sections.text: Intoxication is being drunk. Withdrawal, after heavy regular use, ranges from shakes and anxiety to seizures and delirium tremens, a medical emergency.

sub_sections.title: Alcohol-induced mental disorders
sub_sections.text: Heavy drinking can cause depression, anxiety, psychosis, sleep problems, and lasting memory damage (including Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome). Many improve with abstinence.
